inputs.need:
I am the clinical informatics pharmacist for a three-hospital network that uses one electronic prescribing system. Our drug interaction alerts fire about 21,000 times a month, and prescribers override 94 percent of them. When we looked at 300 overridden alerts, pharmacists judged most of them clinically irrelevant, but 19 were high-severity interactions overridden without any documented reason, including two combinations that led to a patient harm report last year. Prescribers tell us they click through alerts without reading them.

The vendor can switch our system to a tiered display: only high-severity interactions would interrupt the prescriber, and moderate and minor interactions would appear as a passive note in the order summary. We want to find out whether the tiered display makes prescribers respond better to the alerts that matter, without missing moderate interactions that do cause harm. My director wants a randomised comparison rather than a before-and-after switch, because the network is also changing its order sets next year and we would not be able to tell the two apart.

The system can apply the display by ward, and prescribers rotate between wards, so I am not sure whether to randomise wards, prescribers or something else. I need help with the unit of randomisation, the primary outcome (override rates are easy to count but may not mean better care), how to detect harm from suppressed moderate alerts, the sample size, and consent for a trial where prescribers are the participants but patients carry the risk.
inputs.constraints: No additional pharmacist time beyond the existing medication safety team (2.0 FTE). The trial must run within the current vendor contract, which ends in December 2027. The display can be set per ward, not per prescriber.

response.title: Tiered drug interaction alerts and prescriber response: a ward-randomised trial
response.subtitle: Cluster randomised comparison of tiered and standard alert displays across 38 wards
response.statement: Drug interaction alerts fire about 21,000 times a month and 94 percent are overridden, including high-severity interactions overridden without a documented reason. A tiered display that interrupts only for high-severity interactions may improve responses to the alerts that matter, but suppressing moderate alerts could hide harmful combinations. The network needs a randomised comparison because order sets change next year, and the display can be set only by ward while prescribers rotate between wards.
response.whoAffected: Inpatients on 38 wards receiving interacting medicines, especially older adults with kidney impairment; prescribers who face the alerts; the medication safety pharmacists who review harm.
response.whatHurts: A high-severity interaction overridden without thought can cause serious harm; two harm reports last year followed such combinations. Constant low-value alerts waste prescriber time and teach them to click through.
response.currentPractice: Every interaction of any severity interrupts the prescriber with a modal alert; overrides need a free-text reason that is rarely completed.
response.whyNow: The vendor can enable tiering per ward, the harm reports have raised concern, and next year's order set change would confound a before-and-after comparison.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients are protected from dangerous interactions because prescribers notice and act on the alerts that matter.
response.summary: Problem framed as a randomised comparison of alert displays with a harm safeguard for suppressed alerts.

records.title: Tiered drug interaction alerts and prescriber response: a cluster randomised trial on 24 wards
records.authors: Halvorsen-Ibe K, Castaneda-Wright P, Mbeki-Sundqvist L
records.abstract: We randomised 24 wards in two hospitals to a tiered drug interaction alert display or the standard display for six months. With tiering, 29 percent of high-severity interruptive alerts were accepted, compared with 11 percent under the standard display. The number of interruptive alerts per 100 orders fell from 8.2 to 1.9. Pharmacist review found no increase in dispensed moderate-interaction combinations judged harmful. Prescribers rotated between wards, which may have diluted the difference, and adverse drug events were not measured directly.

records.title: Alert override rates in electronic prescribing: a multi-site analysis
records.abstract: Across 9 hospitals, 1.2 million drug interaction alerts were analysed. Override rates were between 90 and 96 percent at every site. High-severity alerts were overridden almost as often as low-severity ones. Override rates rose with the number of alerts a prescriber saw per shift. Reasons were documented for fewer than a third of overrides, and documented reasons were often free text that did not name the interaction. The authors describe alert volume as the main driver of override behaviour. Sites with the highest alert volume also had the highest override rates.

records.title: Interventions to reduce alert fatigue in computerised prescribing: a systematic review
records.authors: Nakashima-Dube T, Ferreira-Olsen A, Varga-Mwangi B, Sato-Holm C
records.abstract: We included 27 studies of tiering, suppression of low-value alerts, redesign of alert text and prescriber-specific filtering. Tiering and suppression reduced alert volume in every study that reported it, and acceptance of the remaining alerts rose in most. Only 4 studies measured patient outcomes, and none found a clear change in adverse drug events. Most studies were before-and-after designs with concurrent changes to prescribing systems. Two randomised studies reported contamination between arms because prescribers worked across units. Few studies reported how long prescribers spent reading alerts.

records.title: Appropriateness of overrides as an outcome in alert trials: a pharmacist review of 1,000 overridden alerts
records.abstract: Two pharmacists independently reviewed 1,000 overridden drug interaction alerts using a written definition of an appropriate override. They judged 87 percent of overrides appropriate, with good agreement (kappa 0.71). Override rates alone misclassified many appropriate overrides as failures and missed inappropriate acceptances. Review took about four minutes per alert. Agreement was lowest for overrides justified by monitoring plans that were not documented in the record. We recommend an outcome that combines accepted alerts and overrides judged appropriate, measured on a random sample when volumes are large.

records.title: Contamination in randomised trials of prescribing decision support when prescribers rotate
records.authors: Brennan-Osei D, Tanaka-Lund F, Reid-Okonkwo G
records.abstract: Using rotation data from 3 hospitals, we simulated trials of a prescribing alert display. When displays were set by ward but prescribers were randomised, 40 percent of orders were exposed to the other arm. Randomising wards reduced exposure to the other arm to under 10 percent but needed a design effect of about 2.1 for the same number of orders. Stratifying by specialty reduced imbalance when there were fewer than 40 wards. We recommend ward-level randomisation whenever the display is a ward setting.

records.title: Harm from suppressed moderate interaction alerts: pharmacist surveillance after tiering
records.abstract: After tiering in one hospital, pharmacists reviewed 2,400 dispensed moderate-interaction combinations over four months. They judged 14 as having caused or contributed to harm (0.6 percent), a rate similar to the year before tiering. Most harms involved potassium-raising combinations in older adults with kidney impairment. The surveillance took about 6 pharmacist hours a week. No harm was judged to have followed a combination that remained interruptive. The authors suggest targeting surveillance at a short list of combinations that caused most harm rather than reviewing every moderate interaction.

records.title: Why prescribers override interaction alerts: a questionnaire study in teaching hospitals
records.abstract: Among 410 prescribers in three teaching hospitals who answered a questionnaire, 72 percent said they overrode interaction alerts without reading them at least weekly. The most common reasons given were that the interaction was already known, that the alert appeared for combinations used routinely, and that the alert text was too long. Junior doctors reported more alerts per shift than consultants. Prescribers supported tiering if high-severity alerts stayed interruptive and were fewer. Consultants were more likely than junior doctors to say that an alert had changed one of their prescriptions in the past month.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One cluster randomised trial found tiering raised acceptance of high-severity alerts from 11 to 29 percent and cut interruptions fourfold, with no rise in harmful moderate combinations. Override rates are uniformly high and uninformative on their own; pharmacist-judged appropriateness is a reliable alternative outcome. Ward randomisation avoids most contamination when displays are ward settings. Surveillance after tiering found harm from suppressed moderate interactions at about the previous rate. No study shows an effect on adverse drug events.
response.gradeRationale: One moderate-quality cluster trial with contamination, a simulation study and observational work; consistent direction for prescriber response, low certainty for patient outcomes.
response.summary: Seven records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Alert volume trains prescribers to override, so high-severity alerts are lost among low-value ones. Tiering removes interruptions for moderate and minor interactions, which should raise attention to the few that remain, but shifts the risk of moderate interactions onto passive notes and pharmacist surveillance. Because the display is a ward setting and prescribers rotate, the unit of randomisation is the ward, and contamination through rotating prescribers will dilute any difference.

response.overview: Two-arm cluster randomised trial: 36 of 38 inpatient wards randomised 1:1 to the tiered or standard drug interaction alert display for six months, stratified by hospital and ward specialty.
response.population: Adult inpatient wards in the three hospitals, excluding the two intensive care units, which use a separate alert configuration; all high-severity interaction alerts raised on participating wards.
response.exposure: Tiered display: high-severity interactions interrupt the prescriber with a modal alert; moderate and minor interactions appear as a passive note in the order summary. Potassium-raising combinations stay interruptive in both arms for patients with reduced kidney function.
response.procedures: The vendor enables the display per ward after randomisation by the trial statistician. Each month, a random sample of high-severity alerts per ward is reviewed by two pharmacists blind to arm where possible, using a written definition of an appropriate response. Pharmacists run targeted surveillance of dispensed moderate combinations from a short list of high-risk pairs in both arms. Prescriber rotation is recorded from the rota system.

outcomes.why: Captures whether prescribers act on the alerts that matter, not just how often they click.

response.feasibility: Double review of about 20 high-severity alerts per ward per month (720 alerts at about four minutes each) takes about 48 hours a month for each of the two reviewers, roughly 0.6 FTE in total, which fits within the 2.0 FTE team only if targeted surveillance is limited to the short list of high-risk pairs.

response.theoreticalFramework: None beyond the trial design; alert fatigue is treated as a volume-attention problem.
response.summary: Ward-randomised trial of 36 wards with an appropriateness primary outcome and harm surveillance.

response.designSummary: Two-arm cluster randomised trial of 36 wards, stratified by hospital and specialty; primary outcome on a monthly random sample of high-severity alerts.
response.sampleSize: About 1,260 high-severity alerts fire each month across the network (about 6 percent of 21,000), roughly 33 per ward; reviewing 20 per ward per month gives about 120 per ward over six months. With an intracluster correlation of 0.05, the design effect is about 7. Detecting an increase in appropriate response from 60 to 69 percent (9 points, more conservative than the retrieved trial's acceptance difference, c1) with 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 needs about 450 alerts per arm before clustering and about 3,150 after, or about 26 wards per arm at 120 alerts each; with 18 wards per arm the trial has about 65 percent power for 9 points and about 89 percent for 12 points. This is the largest trial the network can run, and the estimate is reported with its confidence interval.
response.primaryAnalysis: Mixed-effects logistic regression of appropriate response with a random intercept for ward and fixed effects for the stratification variables; intention to treat by ward allocation.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Negative binomial model for interruptive alerts per 100 orders; harm rate per 1,000 patient days with exact confidence intervals; sensitivity analysis excluding orders by prescribers exposed to both arms.
response.missingData: Sampled alerts that cannot be judged are replaced by the next random alert and counted; wards that close are analysed as randomised for the months they were open.
response.multiplicity: One primary outcome; secondary and balancing outcomes are reported with confidence intervals.
response.software: R with lme4; allocation sequence generated by the trial statistician and concealed until wards are configured.
overfittingGuards: No outcome-driven change to the sampling fraction
Stratification variables as the only covariates
response.summary: Thirty-six wards; about 65 percent power for a 9-point difference and 89 percent for 12 points.

response.risks: Moderate for patients on tiered wards if a suppressed moderate interaction causes harm; low for prescribers. Mitigated by keeping potassium-raising combinations interruptive for kidney impairment and by targeted harm surveillance with a stopping review.
response.consent: Prescribers are the direct participants but cannot opt out of a ward setting; they receive information and can decline alert review of their orders being used for research. Patients are affected indirectly; a waiver of patient consent is requested because the display is a system setting within usual care and individual consent is impracticable, with notices on every ward.
response.data: Alert logs and review forms carry order identifiers only; results are reported by arm, never by prescriber.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older adults, people with kidney impairment and patients on many medicines carry most interaction risk; results are reported for patients aged 75 and over and for reduced kidney function. Junior doctors see more alerts and are over-represented among prescribers; their workload is monitored.
response.effectiveness: The trial decides whether tiering is adopted network-wide before the order set change.
response.efficiency: Uses vendor configuration and existing pharmacist time with sampled review.
response.costs: No vendor cost within the current contract; pharmacist time within the team.
response.partnerships: Prescriber representatives from each hospital, the medication safety committee and two patient partners from the network's patient safety panel.
response.rebPath: Full network REB review under ICH-GCP and Declaration of Helsinki principles, with a request for waiver of patient consent; the REB has not reviewed it yet, and randomisation waits for approval.
response.limitations: Contamination; reviewer unblinding; no adverse drug event outcome; six months only.
response.summary: Cluster trial with a patient consent waiver request, harm surveillance and an unknown REB decision.

response.partnershipPlan: Prescriber representatives and two patient partners review the alert wording and the harm surveillance list before randomisation.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the network's incident reports mentioning alerts from the last two years are read for themes.

response.title: Tiered drug interaction alerts and prescriber response: a ward-randomised trial in three hospitals
response.abstract: Objective: to compare a tiered drug interaction alert display with the standard display. Design: cluster randomised trial of 36 wards, stratified by hospital and specialty, for six months. Primary outcome: appropriate response to high-severity alerts on a pharmacist-reviewed sample. Balancing outcome: harm from moderate interactions. Results will be written after the trial.
response.introduction: Prescribers override almost all interaction alerts, including dangerous ones. Tiering improved response to high-severity alerts in one cluster trial, but no study has shown an effect on adverse drug events.
response.methods: Wards were randomised by the trial statistician, stratified by hospital and specialty. Pharmacists judged appropriateness on monthly random samples, and targeted surveillance covered high-risk moderate combinations in both arms.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the flow of wards and alerts, the primary comparison with its confidence interval, alert burden, harm surveillance and contamination.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret the effect with contamination in mind and weigh it against the harm surveillance. It will state whether tiering should be adopted before the order set change.
response.limitations: Rotating prescribers may dilute the difference, and reviewers may be unblinded. There is no adverse drug event outcome, and follow-up is six months.
response.conclusion: To be written after the trial. It will be limited to prescriber response and harm surveillance.
